summary: This Noba module by Edward Diener and Robert Biswas-Diener explains the replication crisis in psychology, where many published findings, including highly cited ones, fail to replicate. It defines exact and conceptual replication, reviews examples of failed replications such as priming studies, and lists reasons for non-replication including falsified data, small samples, and changing circumstances. It closes by defending risky research and proposing solutions such as public archives of replication attempts, programmatic research, and more skeptical textbooks and journalism.
one_line: Explains why many psychology findings fail to replicate, the types of replication, reasons for non-replication, and proposed solutions.
key_facts: In science, replication is the process of repeating research to determine the extent to which findings generalize across time and across situations.
Exact replication (direct replication) attempts to recreate the methods of an earlier study as closely as possible.
Conceptual replication tests the same hypothesis using a different set of specific methods and measures.
Data reported in 2015 by the Open Science Collaboration, led by Brian Nosek, were published in the journal Science.

Replication rates in the Open Science Collaboration data were 23% for the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (social), 48% for the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 29% for Psychological Science social articles, and 53% for Psychological Science cognitive articles.
Daniel Kahneman, a Nobel Prize-winning psychologist, called the situation in the field a "mess" in an open letter to social psychologists.
In a study of genetics and diseases, only about 4% of gene-disease findings consistently replicated when tested again.
In 1989, scientists reported producing "cold fusion," achieving nuclear fusion at room temperatures, but other scientists were unable to replicate the findings.
Diederik Stapel, a social psychologist in the Netherlands, admitted to faking the results of a number of studies.
Daryl Bem published an article in 2011 claiming that future events could influence the past, and a 2012 paper in the same journal failed to replicate his findings.
Amir and Sharon in 1990 successfully replicated most main effects of six studies from another culture but failed to replicate many interactions.
Psychfiledrawer.org archives attempted replications of specific studies and whether replication was achieved.
Ulrich Schimmack created the Replication Index in 2014, whose "R Index" he describes as a "doping test."
The module argues the academic reward structure, based on publications and prominence, discourages replication.
The module describes the Stanford Prison Experiment and Milgram studies as subjects of textbook inaccuracies identified by Griggs and Whitehead.
